blocks.x: What's going on?
Let's see, let's get your name again. You don't have to touch it. Jeff Bull from Sydney, Australia. And what's your name?
Clotilde Fallon.
And my name is Dick Allen. Alright, how are we doing over there?
Alright.
Good. Let's see, where did we leave off? You were talking about Preservation Hall. Oh yes, impressions of the situation here.

Well, I don't know. I think they're overall much the same because I think the situation is the same. Probably I've accepted the grim fate a bit more than I did last week. All I can say is it's a pity that the last, or the seemingly last stronghold, if you like to call it that of proper music, has to be in those sort of hands. It's a bit of a pity. Anyway, my impressions of the place, as you said last week, have changed because I did that parade on Sunday and heard a church service and all this sort of business. And it does, as you say, it completely changes the outlook on the thing. It was, I really enjoyed it. You weren't there, were you? No, I haven't. This is one up at Harnville. And it was very pleasing to me because it was just like what I hoped it would be like. And they had a Marlis parade with all the fellas in their black suits and black Homburg hats and all the lodge belts and collars and big banners and all that sort of stuff. And all the women were dressed in white and had a big second line and everything. And of course, I was lucky enough to play with the band. And then the church service was something that knocked me right out. Just a local, ordinary church service and a little old wooden church and just sort of, you know, a local housewife's choir. And it was tremendous, phenomenal. That knocked me right out, that church service. The singing was incredible. As I said on the day, if they enjoyed themselves in church like that in Australia, more people would go.
Did they have bowlers on? Any of the men? Derbies? Or was it all Homburg?
I don't know. There might have. I think there were a few. But they were mainly those big black, turned up side Homburgs, you know, that sort of thing.
Anybody take any pictures?

Jules Cahn took some photos and he also took a movie of some of it. Who was in the band, by the way? There was a fella called Brown on Tuba. I don't know his name. Little fella. William Grant. They just call him Brown. Manuel Paul and Andrew Morgan on tenors. Two tenors. No clarinet. I think Andrew Morgan was supposed to play clarinet. I think they expected him to, but he turned up with his tenor. So there were two tenors. Chicken Henry and Earl Humphrey. Booker T. And his son, Papa, I think, what's his name? Noel, isn't it?
Noel Glass.
Noel Glass. Noel was on snare and Booker T. On bass drum. Then there was myself, Sheik and Peter Boccage and this fella, Baptiste, on trumpet.
Milton Baptiste. That's his name.
They just call him Baptiste.
How did the two tenors work together?

Two tenors sounded alright. Sounded quite good. I think it would have been better if there had been a clarinet in there because there was, you know, there was sort of no great contrast in there. But they sounded quite good. Adrian Morgan played pretty well. Is Manuel Paul any good? Manuel Paul's genius, yeah. He's one of my favourite musicians in the city, I think. Amongst about ten or fifteen others. But he is, you know, he's excellent, I think.
Who are your favourites, by the way?

Favourite musicians are Manuel Paul, for one, I don't know what you're just talking about. Captain Handy. George. Lewis. Jim. I like Lewis Nelson very much. I like Jim better. Dee Dee knocked me right out the night I heard Dee Dee. I've only heard him once, but that was tremendous. And Billy, of course, was good. She didn't play on the night, but she sang. And they did a couple of duets, which were really tremendous. I like Kid Thomas. I like Chester's artist very much. And Dre, I've only heard a couple of times, but he played well, I thought. Soi and Sammy Penn are the two best drummers, I think. I don't know who I like the best. I thought, you know, from records, I always thought Soi was better, but Sammy Penn is tremendous in person. Who else is there? Albert Burbank I liked very much. I played one set with him around the Dixieland Hall. I like him. What band was he playing with at Dixieland Hall? Frog Joseph. And I think it was Albert French's band, but Albert French wasn't there.
Brother Conrad wasn't there, huh?

No, no. It was Albert Burbank, Jack Willis, Frog Joseph. Jeanette Kimball played piano. She's good, too. And some fellow called Frank on bass. Frank's somebody or other on bass. Fields, Frank Fields. And Louis Barberin on drums. But who else is there? Well, I like Frank Moyet very much, the piano player. And Charlie Hamilton's also a good pianist. Who else is there? I liked what little he did of Earl Humphrey over the river. Last Saturday he played with the Thomas band over the river at this dance. And he has a bit of a problem with his drinking, I think. And he's out of practice, but he did a few things which were really tremendous.
And what is that dance like over the river?

Well, it was good last week. Very good. It's the first week it had been on. They had a good crowd. It looks as though it's going to kick on. And the band played very well. It's sort of had a bit more life than it does in the hall sometimes. You know, the bands in the hall tend to get a little bit dead, complacent or something. I don't know. But over there they had a bit more life to it. It was going well. Very good.
It was in the band.
Jeff Bull. You were saying there are not many fambon players in town. Well they don't seem to be as I said. Jim's out of town so Lewis Nelson...
This is reel three of Jeff Bull, Friday the 13th of May, 1966. How did we put the date on before?
No, I don't think we did.
Well, we were talking about your career. Where did we leave off? We'd gotten you to England once, huh?
Yeah, that's right.
And back.
I think we were talking about the bands in Australia, the sort of bands they were and things.
Yeah, and the dancing we talked about.
That's right, yeah. Anyway, what happened then? Oh, that's right. Well, from there, you know, I got off the Ken Colgate kick, started the band I had. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

When did these brass bands start really? About three or four years ago I think was the first one at the convention. Of course you have all the old Aiden Monspras and all the old Lou Waters type musicians go, what's all this rubbish, what's this garbage, that's not jazz. Anyway, they started off having one then and they've had one every convention since then but it's always been a sort of very disorganized thing. Last year was the first time we ever got an organization.

But they don't play otherwise, they don't play for funerals or anything. No sir. Do they have friendly societies in Australia, what they call friendly societies in England? Very rarely, very rarely. It's not a very well organized country like here where everybody is organization minded, huh?
No, they don't go very much for that sort of thing. You have Masonic lodges.
For more information visit www.fema.gov Thank you.

segments.title: Reel opening and introductions
segments.summary: Names are confirmed and Allen recalls where the last session left off, on Preservation Hall.

segments.title: Impressions of a parade and church service
segments.summary: Bull describes the parade he played in and a local church service that astonished him, and Allen asks about the hats worn.

segments.title: Parade band personnel and the two tenors
segments.summary: Bull lists the players in the parade band, and they discuss how two tenors worked without a clarinet and Manuel Paul's playing.

segments.title: Bull's favourite New Orleans musicians
segments.summary: Bull names his favourite musicians and drummers and describes sitting in at Dixieland Hall with Albert Burbank's group.

segments.title: The dance over the river
segments.summary: Bull says the new dance across the river had a good crowd and more life than the bands in the hall.

segments.title: Trombone players in town
segments.summary: A fragment about the scarcity of trombone players in New Orleans.

segments.title: Reel three opening and Bull's career so far
segments.summary: Allen dates the reel and recaps the career discussion, and Bull recalls leaving his Ken Colyer phase and starting his own band.

segments.title: Brass bands at Australian conventions
segments.summary: Bull explains how brass bands began at Australian jazz conventions, older musicians' scorn, and the lack of friendly societies.
